title: From 'US innovates, China imitates' to 'Opportunity 2.0' - lessons from Summer Davos
gist: At WEF's Radio Davos debrief of AMNC26 (Summer Davos, Dalian), BCG's Aparna Bharadwaj and ShanghaiTech's Yang Yanqing describe China reframing its rise as 'Opportunity 2.0' rather than a 'China shock,' contrast the US's capital-market-driven AI model against China's vertical, ecosystem-driven approach, and unpack how the Hormuz crisis, AI-driven 'jobless growth' risk and Global South FDI shifts are reshaping policy and investment priorities for the rest of 2026.

insights.claim: China's Premier Li Qiang told AMNC26 business leaders that the world should stop framing China's rise as a 'China shock 2.0' and instead see it as a 'China opportunity 2.0,' a line participants repeatedly referenced during the summit.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals Beijing's deliberate messaging pivot to reassure foreign investors and multinationals that China's tech/manufacturing scale-up should be read as a partnership opportunity, not a competitive threat to hedge against.
insights.quote: we shouldn't be talking about a China shock 2.0, but a China opportunity 2.0
insights.locator: One of the real highlights was the Premier of China

insights.claim: The once-common Western business refrain 'US innovates, China imitates, and Europe regulates' has largely disappeared from conversation over the last decade, as Fortune 500 CEOs now describe both investing in China and competing head-to-head with Chinese companies in global markets.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors benchmarking China-exposure risk should stop pricing China as a low-tech manufacturing base and instead model it as a direct innovation competitor across AI, green tech and beyond.
insights.quote: US innovates, China imitates, and Europe regulates
insights.locator: One of the most common refrains you used to hear 10 years ago

insights.claim: China's innovation model rests on three pillars described by Premier Li Qiang: hard-earned, painstaking internal R&D effort; a 'flying wheel' effect where massive domestic market scale and manufacturing capacity let companies rapidly test whether an innovation works; and a government-nurtured ecosystem and infrastructure base that is not primarily driven by subsidies or IP protection.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: For investors assessing China-based innovation bets, the durable edge is market-scale testing speed and state-built infrastructure, not subsidy arbitrage — a structural moat that is harder for smaller economies to replicate.
insights.locator: Yang Yanqing: Yeah, I think it's a very important issue

themes.theme: Two AI superpowers, divergent funding models

insights.claim: There are effectively two AI superpowers, the US and China, with fundamentally different funding models: the US mobilizes enormous private capital-market resources toward speculative frontier bets (cited examples: SpaceX's IPO and anticipated Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs, including funding unproven concepts like space-based data centers), while China lacks comparably deep capital markets and instead channels more limited resources into vertical, industry-specific AI deployment where it has data and manufacturing advantages.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors should expect US AI outperformance in frontier/moonshot bets funded by public markets, while China-linked AI returns are more likely to show up as productivity/efficiency gains in specific verticals (manufacturing, industrial) rather than breakthrough platform plays.
insights.locator: Yang Yanqing: I think that China's model and United's model is very much a complementary

insights.claim: Middle powers pursuing AI leadership — including Japan, India and Europe — sit between the US and China's two divergent AI funding models (private capital-market-led vs. government/venture-funded with tighter budgets) and are choosing which elements to emulate as they compete for AI talent, IP and innovation leadership.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch which funding model each middle power leans into — capital-markets vs. state-venture — as an early signal of which country's AI ecosystem will scale fastest and where capital should be deployed.
insights.locator: Aparna Bharadwaj: No, of course, I am in violent agreement

insights.claim: China's leading AI frontier models are open source while the comparable US models are closed source, a divergence argued to disproportionately benefit AI adoption and productivity gains across the Global South.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Open-source Chinese AI models could become the default adoption layer for emerging-market enterprises priced out of closed US models, shaping which ecosystem captures long-run developer and enterprise lock-in outside the US/China axis.
insights.locator: Yang Yanqing: Yeah, I think that air quality in China is very much better

insights.claim: Despite more than $250 billion invested in AI in 2025, only about 25% (one in four) of companies report that AI has significantly or drastically changed how they operate, per a Connected World Economic Forum report discussed at AMNC26.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A large gap between AI capex and realized operating-model change suggests near-term AI ROI is being overstated by headline spend figures; investors should discount claims of AI-driven transformation absent evidence of structural workflow change.
insights.locator: Jessica Wanger: 100%. And maybe to kick us off more broadly

insights.claim: Realizing AI productivity gains requires specific organizational preconditions: an 'AI-native,' flatter, modular ('beehive'-like) company structure that can reorganize quickly, adequate prior digitization, and enough trust between human workers and AI agents for the two to collaborate — without these, productivity gains remain elusive even as individual AI use cases succeed.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Screen for these three preconditions (org structure, digitization maturity, worker trust) as leading indicators of which companies will actually convert AI spend into margin expansion versus those merely layering AI on top of legacy processes.
insights.locator: Yang Yanqing: Yeah, thank you, Jessica. A very good questions about AI utilisation

insights.claim: Analysis of online hiring data since ChatGPT's introduction shows individual job tasks have not disappeared, but job postings increasingly bundle multiple tasks that previously belonged to separate roles into single new job descriptions requiring end-to-end process ownership alongside AI.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Labor-market restructuring is happening through job redefinition rather than pure headcount reduction — a signal for HR-tech and workforce-analytics investors to track task-bundling trends rather than simple layoff counts.
insights.locator: I also want to touch upon recent a study from our organisation

insights.claim: Singapore's prime minister framed a core 2026 budget policy goal as 'preventing jobless growth,' reflecting a broader two-speed global economy where a fast-growing tech sector creates fewer, higher-paid jobs while a slower 'Main Street' economy needs broader employment — a top public-policy question now debated across OECD and Global South governments, likely to drive more regulation and economic statecraft.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect rising regulatory intervention (labor rules, AI taxation, industrial policy) aimed at job creation as governments react to AI-driven two-speed growth — a policy risk to price into tech-sector regulatory forecasts.
insights.locator: Aparna Bharadwaj: It's such an interesting question

insights.claim: AMNC26 discussions distinguished '1-10 innovation' (creating a breakthrough new product, which produces proportionately fewer elite jobs) from '10-100 innovation' (scaling a proven innovation to market, which creates substantially more jobs and opportunity) as a framework for how governments and businesses can jointly address job creation from AI-driven change.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Job-creation potential is concentrated in the scaling ('10-100') phase, not the invention phase — investors seeking employment-linked growth themes should favor scale-up/commercialization plays over early-stage breakthrough R&D.
insights.locator: there was an interesting point actually made in the AMNC which talked about 1-10 innovation

insights.claim: China's government is actively supporting the growth of AI-enabled 'one-person companies' as a policy response to help young people cope with AI-driven disruption to entry-level and graduate job markets.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A policy-backed rise in solo AI-augmented micro-enterprises in China could become a template other governments copy to absorb youth unemployment risk from AI displacement — worth tracking for micro-SaaS and solo-founder tooling demand.
insights.locator: another way of the solution is that now China's government is supporting one-person companies

insights.claim: Research on Chinese online hiring data found a roughly four-year lag between what university curricula teach (set based on industry needs at the time of student enrollment) and what employers currently require, because curriculum design cannot keep pace with the speed of technological change.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A structural, multi-year skills-mismatch lag implies persistent graduate underemployment risk even in China's fast-growing tech economy, and highlights recurring demand for corporate/vocational retraining providers to bridge the gap.
insights.locator: we find that if we look at the matching degree of the education content

themes.theme: The cost of AI and the rise of 'frugal AI'

insights.claim: Rising computing costs for AI adoption are starting to offset the economic benefit companies get from replacing human workers with AI, per an audience question at the livestream; CEOs are currently choosing to absorb that expense to drive adoption and employee upskilling, but expect cost-benefit trade-offs to become a bigger explicit decision within a couple of years as deployments move from proof-of-concept to full scale.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Token/compute cost trends are becoming a material input to corporate AI ROI models — investors should monitor inference-cost trajectories as a leading indicator of when AI capex growth could plateau or shift toward efficiency-focused deployment.
insights.locator: Aparna Bharadwaj: I was thinking about the question, it's a good question

insights.claim: Business leaders at Summer Davos coined the term 'frugal AI' — the idea that companies should not deploy AI everywhere at any cost, but should deliberately weigh AI against non-AI solutions, since sometimes AI is not the best or most cost-effective option.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A 'frugal AI' framing among Chinese business leaders suggests China-oriented enterprise AI vendors may compete on cost-efficiency and targeted deployment rather than blanket adoption — relevant for comparing enterprise AI monetization strategies across US vs. China ecosystems.
insights.quote: there's no need for us to try to adopt AI everywhere and at every cost
insights.locator: some business leaders just talk a very interesting terminology, which is the frugal AI

insights.claim: AI costs are expected to fall dramatically over the next five to ten years because the efficiency improvement rate for AI chips and models ('AI's rule') is argued to be faster than Moore's Law, with the ultimate cost floor converging toward the cost of energy/electricity needed to run the systems.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If AI's marginal cost trends toward energy cost, cheap-power regions and utilities become a structural cost advantage for AI deployment — a thesis supporting investment in low-cost energy jurisdictions as AI infrastructure hubs.
insights.quote: the AI's rule is much more efficient than the Moore's rule
insights.locator: Yang Yanqing: Yeah, may I add a few points here?

themes.theme: Energy security after the Hormuz shock

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz crisis is expected to be a policy-shaping geopolitical moment comparable to Fukushima's lasting effect on nuclear policy, reviving interest in renewables and reduced dependence on Gulf oil — but now framed as an energy-security policy question rather than a climate/ESG question.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Renewables and energy diversification investment theses in Asia may now be driven more by security-of-supply logic than ESG mandates, broadening the investor base likely to fund them regardless of climate-policy sentiment.
insights.locator: Aparna Bharadwaj: I think it absolutely has. So if there is going to be

insights.claim: An estimated 10-30% of trade for many Asian economies, particularly across ASEAN, was affected by the elevated cost of energy sourced from the Gulf during the Hormuz disruption.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A double-digit percentage trade exposure to Gulf energy costs across ASEAN quantifies real economic vulnerability, supporting the case for regional energy-diversification and shipping-route hedging investment.
insights.locator: it's all over Asia because many Asian economies were in that bracket

insights.claim: Global shipping choke points are back in strategic focus: Indonesia has discussed instituting a toll on the Strait of Malacca, echoing Iran's stance toward tolling the Strait of Hormuz, raising questions about the UN Charter's free-waterways principle and spurring interest in pipelines and new ports that bypass these choke points.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Emerging chokepoint-toll proposals (Malacca, Hormuz) are a new geopolitical risk factor for shipping and logistics investors, and a tailwind for bypass infrastructure (new ports, pipelines) as insurance against transit-cost escalation.
insights.locator: Shipping lanes is another area. I serve quite a few shipping clients

insights.claim: Even in a best-case scenario where a ceasefire holds and the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens, it is expected to take one to two years for oil and LNG supply to fully normalize because physical infrastructure repairs and supply restoration take time — companies are already planning for this recovery lag, not just for the immediate closure.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Elevated energy costs should be modeled as a multi-year, not a resolved-overnight, risk even after a ceasefire — relevant for energy-cost assumptions in corporate planning and commodity positioning through 2027-2028.
insights.quote: it will take anywhere from one to two years for oil and LNG up to two years to get back to normal supply
insights.locator: even if the perfect outcome happens and we get a ceasefire that holds

insights.claim: As of the July 8, 2026 recording date, oil prices jumped roughly 6% in a single day after Hormuz-related hostilities resumed following what had appeared to be an imminent ceasefire two days earlier.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A real-time example of how fragile the Hormuz ceasefire is — supports maintaining elevated volatility/tail-risk hedges in oil positioning rather than pricing in a swift de-escalation.
insights.quote: it's just gone up 6% because hostilities have restarted
insights.locator: I'm just checking what the oil price is today

insights.claim: China's heavy shift to electric vehicles reduces its exposure to Gulf oil shocks; solar and other new energy sources already account for about 40% of China's total energy supply, but only about 20% of that new energy has so far been integrated onto the electricity grid, indicating significant remaining headroom to expand this buffer against external energy shocks.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: China's large untapped renewable-to-grid integration headroom (only ~20% of new energy on the grid) points to a multi-year domestic buildout opportunity in grid infrastructure and storage as China works to close that gap.
insights.quote: the enrollment of the solar panel and also the new energy has accounted for the 40% of the energy supply in China. But only 20% of new energy have been adopted on the electricity line.
insights.locator: I think that's the China's vision for the green energy

insights.claim: Asked to name the single most important thing to watch for the rest of 2026, Aparna Bharadwaj of BCG picked whether the Strait of Hormuz stays 'open or closed.'
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A senior geopolitics/business advisor's top 2026 signpost is Hormuz status — a simple, trackable binary indicator investors can monitor as a proxy for global energy-risk sentiment for the rest of the year.
insights.locator: Aparna, what's your couple of words that we should be looking out for?

themes.theme: Global South positioning and FDI flows

insights.claim: Global South countries are increasingly positioned as 'swing states' of a fragmented, multipolar world economy — not choosing sides between major powers but working across geopolitical divides, which has made them more strategically important to both the US-led and China-led blocs.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors should treat Global South markets as courted 'swing' jurisdictions likely to receive competing investment offers from both US and China blocs, potentially improving terms and infrastructure access for capital entering these markets.
insights.quote: really a swing state of the world
insights.locator: So I think multipolarity has been an interesting movement for the Global South

insights.claim: The central strategic question for Global South nations is whether they can convert geopolitical 'importance' (as swing states) into true economic 'agency,' which depends on becoming relevant to global supply chains, adopting business-friendly policy, and avoiding economic statecraft that deters foreign investment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Differentiate Global South investment destinations by which are converting swing-state leverage into concrete supply-chain relevance and FDI-friendly policy versus those only gaining diplomatic attention without economic follow-through.
insights.locator: But for emerging markets, the key question I believe

insights.claim: Even though headline global FDI has been declining for a couple of years, greenfield FDI in semiconductors multiplied roughly 7x and in pharmaceuticals roughly 25x, concentrated in nations with the right talent, ecosystem and opportunity.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Headline FDI decline masks a sharp reallocation toward semiconductor and pharma manufacturing capacity — investors should look past aggregate FDI figures and track sector-specific greenfield investment as the real signal of industrial-policy winners.
insights.quote: greenfield FDI in semiconductors multiplied 7x. In pharma multiplied 25x
insights.locator: Take an example of FDI, we discussed in the AMNC

insights.claim: Foreign direct investment into India has tripled over the last five years, driven largely by India's expanding role in global supply chains.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A tripling of India FDI over five years is a concrete, trackable metric supporting continued overweight positioning in India-linked manufacturing and supply-chain plays as a China+1 beneficiary.
insights.quote: FDI into India has tripled in the last five years
insights.locator: FDI into India has tripled in the last five years

insights.claim: Chinese companies are shifting from a pure export/trading mentality ('make in China, trade with the world') to building factories overseas and investing in local talent in Global South markets, because host countries increasingly condition market access on local job creation and investment — mirroring the earlier internationalization path of Western multinationals decades before them.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of Chinese outbound manufacturing FDI into the Global South over the coming years as 'Chinese challengers' localize production — a theme for host-country industrial real estate, local supply-chain, and labor-market investors to track.
insights.locator: So Chinese companies that used to be very focused on the domestic market

insights.claim: The framing of emerging economies as trying to become 'the next China' is misleading: large emerging markets such as India, Brazil and ASEAN nations are instead crafting distinct growth paths suited to a multipolar world — for example a services/LLM-driven model for India and the Philippines, versus a China-linked manufacturing role for Vietnam and Thailand.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Avoid a one-size-fits-all 'next China' investment thesis for emerging markets; instead differentiate exposure by each country's distinct growth model (services/AI for India/Philippines vs. China-linked manufacturing for Vietnam/Thailand).
insights.locator: So this, for me, is a very interesting question to say

insights.claim: ASEAN is moving from a non-binding 'Neutrality Roadmap' set up roughly two to three years earlier toward a formal green-economy framework agreement under Singapore's 2026 ASEAN presidency, reflecting that climate change is treated as an existential rather than academic issue for coastal and island Southeast Asian economies.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A binding ASEAN green-economy framework moving from draft to formal agreement in 2026 is a concrete regional policy catalyst to watch for green-infrastructure and renewable-energy investment across Southeast Asia.
insights.locator: I was reflecting a bit on what I see in the ASEAN forums

insights.claim: China's '30 and 60' carbon strategy (targeting emissions peak and neutrality timelines) has driven the buildout of its EV and solar panel industries, which China credits with supporting both economic growth and improved domestic energy self-sufficiency and security.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: China's carbon-target-driven industrial buildout (EV, solar) functions as dual-purpose economic and energy-security policy, reinforcing continued state support for these sectors regardless of near-term commodity-price cycles.
insights.locator: Thank you for this question. I think that's the China's vision for the green energy

insights.claim: Industrial policy was necessary, not optional, for scaling China's EV market: at the early stage the market was too small and the ecosystem too immature for EVs to reach viability without state support for innovation, manufacturing and investment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Validates the thesis that new-technology sectors requiring large upfront capital and unproven demand (e.g., next-gen batteries, hydrogen) may need similar state-backed industrial policy to reach scale, not pure market forces alone.
insights.locator: And also I want to add a little bit here with regard to the industrial policy

insights.claim: Visible air-quality and noise-pollution improvement was observed in the coastal city of Dalian compared to seven years earlier, attributed largely to the near-disappearance of internal combustion engine vehicles from city streets as EV adoption has surged.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: First-hand, on-the-ground confirmation that China's EV rollout is producing measurable local air-quality benefits supports the durability narrative for China's EV/battery supply chain beyond just export competitiveness.
insights.locator: I did notice in, I came to Dalian seven years ago
